title: Food & drink
goal: Name common foods and drinks, say what you want and what you like, and order a meal.
intro:
Pashtun food is hearty: bread from the clay oven (تنور), rice dishes like **Kabuli palaw**, kebabs, *chapli kabab* in Peshawar, lamb, yoghurt and fresh fruit — and endless cups of green or black tea. The word **ډوډۍ** (ḍoḍə́y) means both 'bread' and 'a meal': ډوډۍ وخورئ 'come and eat!'.

In this unit you'll learn food words, the verbs 'eat', 'drink', 'want' and 'like', and how to order politely.

vocab.note: f · pl: ډوډۍ. Flat bread is also called نان nān.
m. شنه چای 'green tea', تور چای 'black tea'.
f pl — always plural: اوبه سړې دي 'the water is cold'.
m. A hen is چرګه chárga.
f · pl: مېوې. وچه مېوه 'dried fruit and nuts'.
f pl. Diluted salty yoghurt drink: شړومبې shṛúmbe / لسي.
Present stem خور-: خورم xwrəm. Perfective: وخورم wə́xwrəm. Irregular past stem خوړ-.
Present: خوښوم xwaṣawə́m. Adjective خوښ 'liked, pleasing'.
f. Lunch: د غرمې ډوډۍ; dinner: د ماښام ډوډۍ.
m. In Pashto هوټل usually means a place to eat.

phrases.en: I'd like a cup of tea.

phrases.native: دوه پلاوه او يو کباب راوړه.
phrases.roman: dwa palā́wa aw yaw kabā́b rā́wṛa.
phrases.en: Bring two palaws and one kebab.
Put in only a little chilli.

grammar.title: 'I want': غوښتل
grammar.body:
**غوښتل** 'to want' is a regular present-tense verb with the stem **غواړ-** (ġwāṛ-). The present endings, which you will use for almost every verb, are:

زه غواړم ġwā́ṛ-**əm** · ته غواړې ġwā́ṛ-**e** · هغه غواړي ġwā́ṛ-**i**
موږ غواړو ġwā́ṛ-**u** · تاسو غواړئ ġwā́ṛ-**əy** · هغوی غواړي ġwā́ṛ-**i**

With a noun, simply put the thing before the verb: اوبه غواړم 'I want water'. To want to *do* something, use **چې** (che, 'that') and the verb in its perfective form (with و-): غواړم چې ډوډۍ **و**خورم 'I want to eat (lit. I want that I eat)'. You'll learn more about the و- form in units 10 and 17.

examples.en: I want to drink some water.

grammar.title: 'I like': خوښول and خوښ
grammar.body:
There are two common ways to say you like something.

**1. The verb خوښول** 'to like', with you as subject: زه کباب **خوښوم** 'I like kebab'.

**2. The adjective خوښ** 'pleasing' with a possessive clitic — literally 'kebab is pleasing-to-me': کباب **مې خوښ دی**. Here the *thing* is the grammatical subject, so خوښ and the verb agree with it: masculine خوښ دی, feminine **خوښه ده**, masculine plural خوښ دي, feminine plural **خوښې دي**.

The same pattern with the full word زما is also heard: زما چای خوښ دی. Hungry and thirsty are plain adjectives that agree with you: زه وږی يم (m) / زه وږې يم (f).

examples.en: I like tea. (lit. tea is pleasing to me)
He likes sweet things. (خوږ has the irregular plural خواږه)

dialogue.title: Lunch in a Kabul restaurant
dialogue.setting: Bilal and his friend Daud sit down in a busy restaurant. The waiter comes over.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.native: هو، ډېر خوندور پلاو لرو. کباب هم شته.
lines.roman: ho, ḍer xwandawár palā́w láru. kabā́b ham shta.
lines.en: Yes, we have very tasty palaw. There's kebab too.

lines.speaker: Daud
lines.native: زه ډېر وږی يم. ما ته پلاو او کباب دواړه راوړه.
lines.roman: zə ḍer wə́ẓay yəm. mā ta palā́w aw kabā́b dwā́ṛa rā́wṛa.
lines.en: I'm very hungry. Bring me both palaw and kebab.

lines.speaker: Bilal
lines.native: زه يوازې پلاو غواړم، او لږ مستې.
lines.roman: zə yawā́ze palā́w ġwā́ṛəm, aw ləẓ máste.
lines.en: I just want palaw, and a little yoghurt.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: All right. What will you drink?

lines.speaker: Bilal
lines.en: Brother, do you like the palaw?

lines.speaker: Daud
lines.native: ډېر! ډېر خوندور دی. ماړه شوم.
lines.roman: ḍer! ḍer xwandawár day. mā́ṛa shwəm.
lines.en: A lot! It's really delicious. I'm full.

lines.speaker: Bilal
lines.en: How much is the bill, brother?

culture: Hospitality (**مېلمستيا** melmastyā́) is a pillar of Pashtunwali: a guest is fed the best the house has, and refusing food outright can seem rude — say ماړه شوم 'I'm full' and accept at least some tea. Food is eaten with the right hand, often sharing from a common dish on a cloth (دسترخوان) spread on the floor. Green tea is served in small glasses or cups, often with sugared almonds or sweets, and the host will keep refilling: turn your cup over or put your hand over it when you've had enough. In Peshawar's Namak Mandi and Kabul's old bazaars, kebab houses are a social institution.
